first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are internal funnel declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and the inherited record points at signup simplification (memory_31) and onboarding shortening (memory_86) as the interventions that moved exactly those metrics. Fixing a leaking funnel compounds across every acquisition channel, so it is the better bet for sustainable qualified revenue than a price response. I am verifying memory_31 and memory_86 because they are the direct basis for the action I intend to take, and I want the original records to confirm (a) which segment they ran in, (b) whether the lift persisted past week one or decayed, and (c) whether reduced signup fields degraded lead qualification data — a real downstream risk, since fewer fields can raise raw activation while lowering the quality of accounts routed to sales. I am spending the third pull on memory_73 because promotional pricing is the obvious reflex to the competitor's entry pricing and is the highest-risk direction on the list: discount-acquired SMB cohorts can inflate near-term acquisition and revenue while depressing retention, LTV, and reference pricing, and 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' as summarized says nothing about the horizon over which it was measured. If the archive shows memory_73 measured only short-window revenue, that confirms it should not win this slot; if it shows durable margin-positive retention in a matched cohort, I should reconsider. Directions not chosen: memory_57 (referrals) targets established customers and does not address the funnel declines or the competitive threat; memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) is plausibly sound but does nothing for the price-sensitive SMB accounts currently being lost, and the loss is happening now. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout: the inherited claims are consolidated summaries, not re-measured results, and the current declines may reflect a mix shift caused by the competitor rather than a degraded funnel — in which case a funnel fix would underperform its historical effect. I want a controlled read with a holdout and segment splits before committing further capacity, and I am explicitly not treating the historical lifts as guaranteed to replicate at day 76.

final.rationale: Verification changed the ranking within my chosen direction and hardened my rejection of the alternative. exp_73 is now explicitly disconfirmed as a strategy: the 40% discount bought +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue but -12% 30-day retention, with the source record concluding the acquired cohort does not survive first renewal. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching the competitor on price would convert a competitive problem into a churn problem and reset reference pricing for the segment. I decline it despite it being the direct answer to the competitor's move. Within simplify_onboarding, exp_86 (shortened onboarding flow) is the stronger basis than exp_31: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and retention +3% — it is the only verified intervention that improves a funnel metric and retention together, and it maps directly onto the -4% onboarding completion decline, with knock-on effect on the -6% activation decline via time-to-value. So I will run the onboarding-shortening variant, not the signup-field-cutting variant. exp_31 remains supporting evidence but with a caveat I am carrying forward rather than discarding: its activation +9% converted to only +4% qualified revenue with retention -1%, which is the signature of admitting somewhat weaker accounts by removing qualification fields. That gap between activation lift and revenue lift is the downstream risk I flagged pre-verification and it was partly borne out; it is a reason to prefer exp_86's mechanism and to avoid stacking aggressive field removal on top. memory_91 (activation messaging) is compatible and is my fallback if this reads flat, but it is the weaker single bet since it lacks a verified retention or revenue figure. Uncertainty I am not resolving: exp_31 is confirmed on SMB only and did not replicate on other segments, so I should not assume cross-segment generality; and neither source tells me whether the current QoQ declines are a genuine funnel regression or a mix shift caused by the competitor pulling price-sensitive accounts out of the top of funnel. If it is mix shift, a funnel fix will underperform its historical effect. Standard experiment with a holdout and SMB-versus-other segment splits, tracking 30-day retention and qualified revenue as primary rather than completion or activation alone — the exp_73 record is a direct warning against reading a top-of-funnel lift as a win. Not chosen: promotional_pricing (disconfirmed above), referral_incentive (memory_57 targets established customers, addresses neither decline), enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44 is plausible and unverified, and does nothing for the SMB accounts being lost now).
